newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU faces diplomatic headache over EMU members.
newsitem.headline: EU faces diplomatic headache over EMU members.

text.p: Europe is approaching the point of no return on the way to a single currency, but still faces tough questions over a drive by Italy, Spain and Portugal to be in from the start in 1999.

Where will the currency zone mark out its southern frontier? Will it restrict membership to northern-European states to guarantee the credibility of the euro from the start, or will it include Mediterranean economies which are seen as less stable?

Even more complicated, officials and economists say, is deciding if Spain and or Portugal, whose chances of meeting Maastricht treaty criteria look higher than Rome's, can be included without seriosuly offending EU founding member Italy.

Economists say it will be difficult for Germany, already reluctant to give up its cherished mark, to accept Italy from the start. Italy would find it hard to accept being left out if Spain and Portugal join.
"It would be diplomatically and politically difficult to have Spain and Portugal in and Italy out," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
Officials are avoiding public comment on the question, repeating that a decision will be made in early 1998 on which countries qualify to join the euro in 1999.

But a diplomatic offensive is likely to be stepped up this year to find a solution which will satisfy all sides and prevent a financial market crisis if any, or all, of the three are left out initially.
Economists say it is in nobody's interest to have a public brawl over the issue, and that some kind of diplomatic solution is likely to be found before the 1998 decision.
"The least likely of all scenarios is that it ends in an argument," Williams said.

He said the solution could include strong public statements of support for those waiting to join, the so-called "pre-ins", for example promising them membership of European monetary union (EMU) before notes and coins go into circulation in 2002.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told reporters on Monday the EU should define the difference between the "pre-ins" and those unlikely, or unwilling, to join near-term.
These "pre-ins" could take part in a special council proposed by France to co-ordinate economic policies inside the euro zone after the launch of monetary union, he said.
A new Exchange Rate Mechanism to link currencies outside monetary union to the euro -- agreed in Dublin in December -- is also meant to anchor the "pre-ins".

Ensuring a cliffhanger finish to the diplomatic juggling over Spain, Italy and Portugal however is the fact that Germany itself is struggling to reduce its deficit below three percent of Gross Domestic Product this year, the key year for deciding which countries join the euro in 1999.
"Without a considerable acceleration in economic growth, Germany will fail to meet the deficit criteria," former Bundesbank President Karl-Otto Poehl told a conference in Paris earlier this month.
But Germany is in the difficult situation of having told its European Union partners EMU's founding Maastricht treaty must be interpreted strictly. "It's a little ugly," Poehl said.
One European source said however that Germany would do everything possible to "get on the right side of three percent".
France, meantime, whose own budget deficit looked likely a year ago to overshoot the Maastricht target, is for the time being at least, cruising fairly smoothly towards monetary union.
A Reuters poll of 21 economists last week showed the vast majority clustered around a forecast that the French deficit would be 3.0 percent of GDP this year.
